title: Infra: GPU Fleet, Capacity Planning, IaC Modules, and CI/CD Playbook
author: Liam Chen
content:
Summary:
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s operational guidance for the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking requirements, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipelines, and the core infra runbooks the team uses for day-to-day operations. It is intended as the canonical reference for infrastructure engineers onboarding to GPU/cluster work, and for service owners who need to understand constraints and knobs when deploying inference workloads.

Audience:
- Infra engineers owning GPU fleet and autoscaling
- SREs responsible for capacity and SLOs
- Platform engineers maintaining Terraform/IaC modules
- Service owners planning model-serving footprints

Goals and scope:
- Describe capacity planning process and target metrics (utilization, queue latency, p95 token latency)
- Define cloud account layout and VPC/networking patterns for Dedicated/Private deployments
- Provide conventions and examples for Terraform modules and IaC testing
- Document CI/CD pipeline templates for model-serving services and GPU node images
- Include operational runbooks for common incidents and scale events

1) GPU fleet and capacity planning
Intro:
Our GPU fleet supports inference clusters across hosted and dedicated offerings. The fleet is organized by instance classes (low-latency, throughput, quantized, and experimental). Capacity planning balances cost and latency; we use demand forecasting + safety buffers to size pools.

Key metrics and targets:
- Cluster utilization (per-instance vGPU): target 55-70% average; avoid sustained >80%
- Queue latency: p95 request queueing < 30ms for low-latency pools
- P95 token generation latency (observed at API layer): <= configured SLO per route (e.g., 200ms for 128-token requests on gN5.2x)
- Scale-up time: target cold scale from 0 to fully joinable instances < 6 minutes (where possible)

Forecasting process (quarterly + ad-hoc):
1. Pull usage per route (tokens, concurrency) for last 90 days from observability dashboards.
2. Apply growth model (baseline + 20% conservative multiplier or business-provided forecast).
3. Identify peak-hour requirements and derive required concurrent tokens/sessions.
4. Add safety buffer: +15% for predictable workloads, +30% for unvalidated workloads.
5. Produce capacity request and submit to procurement/finance for Reserved Capacity commits.

Autoscaling and pooling patterns:
- Dedicated pools: pinned instances with autoscale headroom for burst. Use scheduled scaling for predictable daily patterns.
- Shared hosted pools: dynamic scaling with conservative minimums per region. Implement spillover routing to secondary regions when utilization > 85%.

2) Cloud accounts and networking
Account topology:
- Management account: global infra services (CI/CD runners, state backends, cross-account IAM administration).
- Region accounts: one account per major cloud region (us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) to satisfy data residency and fault isolation.
- Customer-dedicated accounts: for Private deployments we create customer-specific accounts/projects with restricted cross-account access.

VPC and subnet conventions:
- VPC per account and environment (prod/staging/dev).
- Subnet segmentation: public (load balancers), private (services), gpu-subnets (isolated for GPU instances with accelerated networking enabled).
- Network ACLs: deny by default; open only required ports (SSH only from bastion / jump host IPs, control plane ports between services).

Egress and peering patterns:
- Use VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, and metadata where possible to avoid public egress.
- Transit gateway for cross-VPC routing between control plane and region accounts.
- Use service mesh egress policies for telemetry flows to observability endpoints.

Security controls:
- NSGs and host-based firewalls on GPU nodes to limit inbound control plane traffic.
- IAM roles scoped to least privilege; cross-account role trust only to named service principals.
- KMS/HSM usage for model artifacts stored in S3 buckets with bucket-level access logging and object-level encryption.

3) Terraform / IaC modules and conventions
Module layout and ownership:
- Modules live in git under infra/terraform/modules. Each module has a README, examples/, and a test/ directory with terratest or kitchen-terraform harnesses.
- Ownership: every module must include a CODEOWNERS entry and an oncall owner definition.

Naming and variable conventions:
- Resource names: short, kebab-case, include environment and region (e.g., rdx-gpu-pool-prod-usw2).
- Variables: avoid dynamic defaults that depend on remote state; prefer explicit inputs.
- Outputs: expose IDs and ARNs necessary for cross-module wiring, but do not export credentials.

Module example (GPU autoscaling group):
```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source            = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-terraform-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
  name              = "rdx-gpu-pool-prod-usw2"
  instance_type     = "g5.2xlarge"
  min_size          = 2
  max_size          = 50
  target_utilization = 0.6
  subnets           = var.gpu_subnets
  tags = {
    service = "serving"
    owner   = "infra"
  }
}
```

Testing and continuous validation:
- All modules must include unit-style tests in test/ and integration tests using ephemeral accounts where possible.
- PRs must run: terraform fmt, tflint, plan (with diff annotations), terratest/kitchen tests for resources the PR affects.

State management and drift detection:
- Remote state backends: use a central S3 bucket with state locking via DynamoDB (or equivalent).
- Periodic drift detection: weekly terraform plan runs in a CI job flagged to infra-ops if unexpected diffs appear.

4) CI/CD and build pipelines
Pipeline patterns for infra and bake images:
- Single-purpose pipelines: one pipeline per job (e.g., module-test, module-apply, gpu-image-bake).
- Gate rules: all applies to prod require 2 approvers from infra or platform on-call and an automated preflight check that validates cost impact and security scan.

Example GitHub Actions job for module PRs:
```yaml
name: terraform-pr
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint-and-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
      - name: terraform fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check
      - name: tflint
        run: tflint
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${{ secrets.TF_STATE_BUCKET }}"
      - name: terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - name: upload-plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan
```

Image bake and AMI lifecycle:
- Golden image pipeline builds GPU AMIs/VM images weekly or on-demand for security patches. Use Packer with inline tests to validate CUDA, drivers, and runtime libraries.
- Images are versioned and promoted across staging -> canary -> prod with automated deployment jobs that update autoscaling group launch templates.

Release process for infra applies:
1. Module or stack PRs target staging. Run full integration tests.
2. On approval and green tests, merge to main.
3. Auto-trigger canary applies to a single region account with monitoring checks for 30 minutes.
4. If canary passes, automated rollout to remaining regions with staggered waits and health checks.

5) Runbooks (operational playbooks)
Runbook: GPU node OOM or CUDA driver failures
- Symptoms: increased FATAL logs on compute nodes, kubelet evictions, or repeated container restarts tied to GPU allocation.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Identify affected nodes: kubectl get nodes -l rdx-gpu=true --show-labels and kubectl describe node <node> for Allocatable/GPU metrics.
  2. Move traffic: cordon node(s) and drain with --ignore-daemonsets for graceful termination.
  3. Restart GPU driver daemonset: kubectl rollout restart ds/nvidia-driver -n kube-system.
  4. If driver restart fails, reprovision node via ASG replace-instance or terminate the instance to trigger fresh launch.
- Postmortem steps:
  - Collect logs (/var/log/nvidia-installer.log, dmesg, kubelet logs) and attach to incident.
  - Create a bug for root cause and track remediation (e.g., driver version pin, image fix).

Runbook: Sudden capacity shortfall (high queueing, autoscale lag)
- Symptoms: sustained queue depth increase, high 5xxs for routing service, autoscaler hitting max_size.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Confirm metrics: check autoscaler metrics, ASG desired/actual, and cluster CPU/GPU utilization dashboards.
  2. Temporarily increase max_size for affected pool via terraform variable override and trigger apply (manual playbook input required).
  3. If immediate headroom needed, failover routing: enable spillover to secondary region using routing policy in control plane (see routing-runbook).
  4. Notify SRE and on-call capacity engineer; open incident channel and track expected recovery ETA.
- Post-incident:
  - Reconcile scaling events with forecast; update scaling policy or submit Reserved Capacity request if shortfall persists.

6) Team wiki and onboarding checklist
Core wiki pages to read first:
- GPU capacity and infra runbook (this doc)
- Terraform/IaC and modules README
- Golden images and bake pipeline docs
- Networking and account topology guide

Onboarding checklist (for new infra engineers):
1. Read this playbook and the GPU runbook referenced in related_pages.
2. Get access to management account and observability dashboards (Grafana, Prometheus, SLO dashboard).
3. Run a local terraform plan against a sandbox account and execute module tests.
4. Shadow a capacity planning meeting and review past quarter forecasts.
5. Practice of incident runbook steps in a game-day exercise.

Appendix: Examples and useful commands
- Check GPU node health:
  kubectl get nodes -l rdx-role=gpu -o wide
  kubectl top nodes --selector=rdx-role=gpu
- Scale a module temporarily (example override):
  terraform apply -var="gpu_pool_max=80" -target=module.gpu_node_pool
- Run image bake (packer):
  PACKER_LOG=1 packer build -var-file=variables.pkr.hcl gpu-ami.pkr.hcl

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity (oncall: infra-capacity-rotation)
- Secondary owner: eng-sre oncall
- Pager escalation: infra oncall -> platform lead -> VP infra after 60 minutes of unresolved P1

Related references
- infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (detailed module reference)
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (operational playbook examples)

Document maintenance
- This page is reviewed quarterly around capacity-planning cycles and after major infra incidents.
- Make small edits directly and tag reviewers for substantive changes.

End of document.
